name: CT-RATE
description: A public open-source dataset that pairs non-contrast 3D chest CT volumes with corresponding radiology text reports. CT-RATE comprises 25,692 scans from 21,304 unique patients and includes reconstructed 3D chest CT volumes, radiology reports, anonymized metadata, extracted multi-abnormality labels for 18 abnormalities, and organ-level anatomical segmentation labels generated using a state-of-the-art segmentation model.
creator: Ibrahim Ethem Hamamci
citeAs: Ibrahim Ethem Hamamci. CT-RATE: Paired chest CT volumes and radiology reports. https://huggingface.co/datasets/ibrahimhamamci/CT-RATE. 2025.
rai:dataCollection: The dataset was curated from chest CT volumes and corresponding radiology text reports from Istanbul Medipol University Mega Hospital. It includes non-contrast chest CT volumes acquired between May 2015 and January 2023, totaling 50,188 reconstructed CT volumes from 25,692 distinct CT experiments conducted on 21,304 unique patients. Every reconstructed volume from the hospital database was incorporated. Reports were anonymized by removing personal information pertaining to patients and medical professionals, translated from Turkish to English using the Google Translate API, and reviewed and corrected by bilingual final-year medical students. CT volumes were quality controlled by excluding volumes involving contrast material or body parts other than the chest, standardizing orientation, and removing identifying information from metadata.
rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Software Collection, Manual Human Curator
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw data consist of chest CT volumes and corresponding radiology text reports from Istanbul Medipol University Mega Hospital. The CT-RATE dataset contains the original raw data. Reports include clinical information, technique, findings, and impression sections. Associated metadata were also collected and anonymized.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Reports were anonymized using targeted searches with regular expressions to identify and eliminate date-related information and patient-doctor identifiers, then translated from Turkish to English using the Google Translate API and reviewed by bilingual final-year medical students. CT volumes were filtered to exclude contrast studies and non-chest body parts, orientation was standardized using metadata, and identifying information was removed from metadata. Similar conditions were grouped during report annotation, such as left and right mucoid impactions under mucoid impaction, various lung opacities under lung opacity, and lung and fissural nodules under lung nodules.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Each volume was resized to uniform spacing of 0.75 mm in the x-axis and y-axis and 1.5 mm in the z-axis. CT volumes were then center-cropped or padded to a consistent resolution of 480×480×240. Volumes were converted to Hounsfield Unit values using intercept and slope values from metadata, clipped to a range of -1000 to 1000, and normalized during training to a range of -1 to 1. Identical preprocessing was applied to external datasets for evaluation.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Within CT-RATE, 1,000 reports were manually annotated for 18 distinct abnormalities by merging findings and impression sections into a multi-label dataset. Conditions not referenced in either section were considered absent. The annotated reports were split into training (800) and validation (200) sets and used to finetune the RadBERT-RoBERTa-4m model, which was then applied to classify the remaining 24,692 reports and extract global abnormality labels. In addition, bilingual final-year medical students reviewed and corrected translated reports and removed residual personal information. Organ-level anatomical segmentation labels were generated using a state-of-the-art segmentation model.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The manually annotated 1,000 reports were split into training and validation sets for finetuning the automated label extractor. The finetuned text encoder's precision, recall, and F1 scores are reported, showing robust classification across abnormalities. Similar conditions were grouped into broader abnormality categories, and conditions not referenced in findings or impression were considered absent.
rai:annotationsPerItem: For report abnormality annotation, 1 label set per report covering 18 abnormalities
rai:annotatorDemographics: Bilingual final-year medical students; three board-certified radiologists evaluated report generation outputs
rai:machineAnnotationTools: Google Translate API, RadBERT-RoBERTa-4m, TotalSegmentator, state-of-the-art segmentation model
rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The dataset is publicly accessible via Hugging Face. The authors state plans to extend CT-RATE with multi-abnormality segmentation and localization labels for 3D chest CT volumes as future work. Trained models and code are publicly available in GitHub repositories.
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Patient age, sex, clinical information, medical history, symptoms, scan metadata, and geography/institutional origin. Reports originally contained personal information pertaining to patients and medical professionals, which was removed during anonymization.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The paper states that the open-source release of CT-RATE, CT-CLIP, and CT-CHAT addresses critical challenges in 3D medical imaging, lays the groundwork for future innovations in medical AI, may enhance radiologists’ workflows, reduce time and effort required for interpretation, improve diagnostic accuracy, support educational and clinical research settings, and ultimately contribute to improved patient care.
rai:dataBiases: The authors state that biases inherent to the single-institution dataset may influence self-supervised training. Although the dataset is large and diverse, the data originate from a single geographic and clinical setting, which may limit generalizability to other populations. The paper also notes that CT-CLIP depends on the specific terminology used in reports and the choice of prompts during zero-shot detection, and variability in how diseases are described across radiology reports can affect detection accuracy.
rai:dataLimitations: The dataset is single-center and may have limited generalizability to other populations. The current models are limited to chest CT volumes only. CT-CLIP depends on report terminology and prompt choice. The evaluation of CT-CHAT is limited by the lack of pretrained 3D medical multimodal AI assistants for benchmarking, leading to comparisons against 2D models using DRRs. The quality of generated reports remains insufficient for clinical use, and the models are far from ready for clinical deployment. The paper also notes that detailed metadata for the private UPMC external validation set are not publicly available.
rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is used for training and internal validation of CT-CLIP and CT-CHAT, zero-shot multi-abnormality detection, supervised baseline training, finetuning, volume-to-volume retrieval, report-to-volume retrieval, report generation, and creation of a visual question-answering dataset with over 2.7 million question-answer pairs derived from CT-RATE. The authors also state that organ-level anatomical segmentation labels may support tasks such as visual grounding and anatomical localization.
